title: Report on Studying Abroad at the University of Freiburg
paragraphs: I was allowed to study at Freiburg University in Germany from 2018/04/03 to 06/22. Freiburg is located in southwestern Germany, a city rich in nature surrounded by the Black Forest. It has a beautiful old town where a medieval atmosphere remains strongly. It seems to be a popular city even within Germany, and I heard that housing costs are as high as in big cities such as Berlin and Munich. It was also safe, about the same as Japan in the daytime, so I actually found it very comfortable to live in.

Regarding the clerkship, in April I trained in neurosurgery at the university hospital for four weeks, in May in anesthesiology for four weeks at a community hospital in Freiburg (RKK Klinikum Loretto Krankenhaus), and in June I went back to the university hospital and trained in neuroradiology for three weeks.

The first, neurosurgery, was housed in the neurological disease center (Neurozentrum) in Freiburg University Hospital, a department boasting a scale among the largest in Europe, with six operating rooms dedicated to neurosurgery and about 3000 cases a year, and doctors came to learn not only from Germany but also from various countries such as Italy and Sweden. The clerkship started with the morning conference at 7 o'clock, followed by observing surgery and ICU management, and receiving lectures that the doctors occasionally gave. Because the number of cases was large, I went in and out of the operating room as my interests led me, for brain tumours and neuroendovascular treatment and so on. Because the conferences were all in German there was much I could not understand, but if I asked the doctors in English afterwards, they kindly taught me. A Swedish doctor who looked after me also gave me words of encouragement such as, "With the language barrier it must be hard, but you do not need to understand everything, so work while being conscious of what you should learn as a student." Also, in a division called Functional Neurosurgery, different from the General Neurosurgery to which I was assigned, deep brain stimulation (DBS) for Parkinson's disease and so on was performed, and although it was not my assigned division, it was a field I was interested in, so when I negotiated directly with the professor, he kindly let me see it and taught me carefully, with related papers as well. The neurosurgeons were busy and did not often take care of me on their own initiative, but if I asked actively myself they would teach me, so it became a first clerkship in which proactiveness was tested.

In May I rotated through anesthesiology at the community hospital mentioned above, Loretto Hospital. Loretto Hospital is apparently one of the teaching hospitals associated with Freiburg University, and I was told that quite a few local students visit. It was a beautiful brick hospital with a Christian foundation, with a more relaxed, homelike atmosphere than the university hospital. It seems I was the first exchange student from Japan, and I was welcomed warmly. It started with the 7 a.m. conference, after which I went into several operating rooms and, attached closely to a senior doctor, was taught in detail about how to use the equipment, how to administer drugs, how to read ECGs and how to take physical findings. Because I retain nothing of anesthesiology studied from textbooks alone, being taught one-on-one was a very valuable opportunity. Also, since it was a community hospital, under the doctor's guidance I was allowed to experience procedures such as tracheal intubation, manual mask ventilation and line placement, and by the end of the clerkship I had become quite used to them, so I was told "You have improved a lot!" In spare time, I talked about various things with the doctors and operating room nurses in the break room while drinking warm soup (all you can drink). There was also a doctor who had previously studied in Japan, and on days off I was taken to a beer garden. At this outside hospital I also met local students. Several came to train from other German cities such as Hanover and Kiel, and after the clerkship we went to a nearby rock bar and music festival and had a good time.

For the last three weeks, I returned to the university and rotated through neuroradiology, a department that does not exist in Japan. It is a department housed in the same neurological disease center (Neurozentrum) as the neurosurgery I rotated through in April, and since besides reading brain and spinal images it also does endovascular treatment for cerebral infarction, my impression was that it is more subdivided than in Japan. After the morning conference, the doctor assigned me several cases, and I read the images myself, summarised the findings and presented, and so on, experiencing various cases. Besides stroke and various neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's, being in Europe, it was impressive that there were many patients with multiple sclerosis (MS). When I got tired of reading images, I observed catheter treatment or received a stroke lecture mixed in with the local students, and it became a clerkship with a great deal of learning. In fact, I had entered the country without the June clerkship department decided before leaving, but when I consulted a neurosurgery doctor, he told me about the existence of this neuroradiology department. I went to negotiate directly at the professor's office without an appointment, and I got an OK the same day, so I think this too depends on one's own actions.

In time outside the clerkship, I had fulfilling times such as going to beer gardens with local students and being invited to their homes for parties. Also, since I lived in a shared house, I interacted with people not only from Germany but from various countries. I was astonished at the breadth of vision of people not so different in age from me, such as a Latvian engineer who speaks five languages and flies around Europe, and a Slovenian nurse who had also served in Afghanistan as NATO staff. When I had a stretch of days off, I travelled in Germany and to other European countries. Because the borders with Switzerland and France are close, access was also good. Since I was originally interested in Western painting and history, I toured sightseeing spots across Europe and had a very luxurious time.

Looking back, I feel once again that these three months were a very valuable experience for me. In the local clerkship there were times when I thought the study I had done at pre-departure training sessions was useful, but more often I felt my own lack of ability in both language and knowledge. I definitely want to make use of this in my studies from now on, and in the sense of having gained that kind of stimulus too, there was a great harvest.

Finally, I would like to take this opportunity to thank Dr. 粕谷, Dr. 長谷川 and the other doctors of the International Collaboration Office, the academic affairs staff, the doctors in Freiburg who gave me great support from the preparation of the study abroad through to after my return, and 大道-kun, with whom I spent the three months. Thank you very much indeed.
